name: Anxiety and generalised anxiety disorder
definition: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is a long-term condition in which a person feels worried or anxious about many different things, much of the time.
overview: Everyone feels anxious from time to time, and Mind says this does not mean a person has a mental health problem. Anxiety becomes a problem when it is felt a lot, for months at a time, or comes with panic attacks. Generalised anxiety disorder is a long-term condition marked by worry about many different things rather than one event. Talking therapies, self-help and medicines can all help.
causes: The exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and it is likely that several factors play a part.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists says there is no single origin, and genes, social environment and life experiences all contribute and interact.
Differences in brain activity and in brain chemicals such as serotonin and noradrenaline have been described.
riskFactors: Having another anxiety disorder, such as panic disorder or social phobia.
Having close relatives with an anxiety disorder.
Having depression or another mental health condition.
A history of stressful or traumatic experiences.
Living with a long-term painful health condition.
GAD is more common in women than in men.
complications: Worry that affects daily life and is hard to control.
diagnosis: A GP can diagnose GAD from a person's symptoms. The GP asks questions about symptoms and worries. They may also check for other causes, such as thyroid problems or side effects of medicines.
treatment: The NHS says people are usually advised to try psychological treatment before medicine. Options include self-help books or online courses, guided self-help based on cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and CBT with a therapist. If these do not help, a medicine is usually offered, and the usual first choice is a type of antidepressant called an SSRI. Regular exercise and calming breathing exercises are also suggested.
prevention: There is no sure way to prevent GAD, but seeking help early and using self-help approaches such as exercise and breathing exercises may help.
seekCare: If anxiety affects daily life or causes distress, a routine GP appointment is the usual first step. In England adults can also refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service without a GP referral. If someone is in crisis but not in immediate danger, NHS 111 has a mental health option that can be called any time, free of charge. If there is an immediate risk to life, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 to talk to someone.

sections.heading: What is anxiety, and what is generalised anxiety disorder?
sections.body:
Anxiety is the feeling that comes with worrying about something that could happen. Mind says that feeling anxious from time to time does not mean a person has a mental health problem. It can become a problem when a person feels anxious a lot of the time, or for months at a time, or has panic attacks.

Generalised anxiety disorder, often shortened to GAD, is a long-term condition. A person with GAD feels worried or anxious about many different things, rather than about one particular event. The worry is hard to control and affects daily life. There are other anxiety disorders too, such as panic disorder and social phobia, which the NHS lists separately.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of GAD?
sections.body:
GAD affects both the mind and the body. The main feature is feeling worried or anxious much of the time in a way that is hard to control. Psychological symptoms can include restlessness, feeling on edge, irritability and difficulty concentrating.

Physical symptoms can include trouble sleeping, tiring easily, dizziness and a pounding or fluttering heartbeat known as palpitations. Some people also feel muscle tension or have stomach problems. Not everyone has every symptom, and the mix can differ between people. Symptoms can make it hard to relax, to switch off from worrying thoughts, or to feel rested after a night's sleep. Because symptoms vary from person to person, the NHS has a separate page on the signs of an anxiety disorder.

sections.heading: What causes generalised anxiety disorder?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, but several factors probably play a part. The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes no single origin, with genes, social environment and life experiences all contributing and interacting. It adds that having a close relative with GAD raises a person's risk, but that no single gene is responsible.

Other things linked with GAD include having another anxiety disorder, depression, or a history of stressful or traumatic experiences. Living with a long-term painful health condition is also listed. Some sources point to differences in brain activity and in brain chemicals such as serotonin and noradrenaline. None of this means a person is to blame for feeling anxious.

sections.heading: How is GAD diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP can diagnose GAD based on a person's symptoms. At the appointment the GP asks questions about the symptoms and the worries behind them. They may also look for other possible causes, such as thyroid problems or side effects from a medicine.

NICE guidance describes a stepped approach, starting with identifying and assessing the problem, explaining what GAD is and what treatments exist, and active monitoring. It says education and monitoring alone can suit people whose distress is mild and who have little difficulty in daily life. The GP may then talk through the options for help with the person, including self-help, talking therapies and medicines. Anyone worried about their own symptoms can talk to a GP about them.

sections.heading: How is GAD treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says people are usually advised to try psychological treatment before being prescribed medicine. NICE describes low-intensity options first, such as self-help, guided self-help or group sessions that teach about anxiety. If these are not enough, it describes higher-intensity treatment: CBT or applied relaxation, or a medicine. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says CBT helps people test their fears and learn to tolerate anxiety.

The usual first medicine is a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, which is also used for anxiety. NICE says benzodiazepines should not usually be offered, other than briefly during a crisis. Treatment can take time to work, and symptoms may come back. Antipsychotic medicines are not to be offered for GAD in primary care.

sections.heading: Living with anxiety and what helps
sections.body:
The NHS suggests self-help such as books, online tools or courses that can be done in a person's own time. Regular exercise and calming breathing exercises are also recommended. NHS Every Mind Matters suggests mindfulness, and setting aside a daily time for worries if worry takes over the day. It also says that avoiding situations can make anxiety worse, so gradually facing them is often recommended.

GAD is a long-term condition, so the outlook is usually one of managing it over time. Many people find that talking therapies, self-help and medicines help, though symptoms can return. Talking with a GP or a talking therapies service can help a person decide which approaches suit them. Charities such as Mind offer information and support.

sections.heading: When should someone get help?
sections.body:
If anxiety affects daily life or causes distress, the NHS advises seeing a GP, which is a routine appointment. In England an adult can also refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP, though details vary by area.

If someone is in crisis but not in immediate danger, they or a person close to them can call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, which is free and available at any time. Where there is an immediate risk to life, call 999 or go to A&E. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 for anyone who needs someone to talk to. NHS 111 mental health is not an emergency service, and it cannot arrange hospital admissions or give a diagnosis.

faqs.q: Is feeling anxious the same as having an anxiety disorder?
faqs.a: No, Mind says feeling anxious from time to time does not mean a person has a mental health problem. Anxiety may be a problem when it is felt a lot, lasts for months, or comes with panic attacks. A GP can help to work out what is going on and what could help.

Yes, there are several treatments. These include self-help, talking therapies such as CBT, and medicines, usually an SSRI antidepressant. Treatment can take time to work, and symptoms may return. The NHS says people are usually advised to try psychological treatment before medicine.

faqs.q: Do I need a GP referral for talking therapy?
faqs.a: In England adults can usually refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without a GP referral. Some services take phone or online referrals and others ask for a GP referral, so it is worth checking the local service. Adults can also see a GP, who can talk through the options.

faqs.q: Does a family history of anxiety mean someone will develop GAD?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says having a close relative with GAD raises risk, but no single gene is responsible. Genes, social environment and life experiences all contribute. The Royal College describes several genes with small individual effects that combine to raise risk. The NHS says the exact cause is not fully understood.

faqs.q: Who can someone talk to in a crisis?
faqs.a: Anyone in immediate danger should call 999. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option, free and available at any time. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123. A GP appointment is the routine route for ongoing anxiety. NHS 111 mental health is not an emergency service.
